Of course it is ;-) as all computing is math, and the screen is a
coordinate system. Only question is: Are the 'crazy patterns'
computed out of a formula, or just taken from a table, or a simple
algorithm?

Example: Be P a point (x;y) of the screen symbolizing a bullet. Be v
its velocity (in horizontal direction; unit is pixel per frame) and
a the (vertical) acceleration ('gravity'). We start at the top left
(co-ordinate 0;0) and count pixels to the lower and right border.

'Bronshtein's Book of Physical Formula's' [1] says:

P is a function of time t; Px = vt ; Py = a t²

but the programmer says:

Set Px, Py and vy to zero (vy is vertical velociy- we start at
zero). Consider a and v as measured in terms of pixels for length
unit and frames as time unit. Every frame do:

Add Px with v and store to Px
Add Py with vy and store to Py
Add vy with a and store in vy
Put the bullet sprite at its new position Px;Py

Done.

That would be a simple algotithm- in fact, we made use of advanced
physics and a bit of differential analysis- but we end up with three
additions! One to the right, a few down...

>  Come on, don't tell me that's more
> "1 pixel down, two left" stuff.

Advanced reading here, especially example 6 for how to draw a
straight line between two pixels (which, of course, also is the
basis of 'shooting in arbitrary direction at Adam's sprite')

http://www.worldofspectrum.org/ZX81BasicProgramming/chap18.html

> > Please don't say "the math was worked out
> > beforehand and put into a table."  It's still
> > some kind of equation...

Of course you can do a proper y; sin(y) table (instead of our
gravity acceleration above) to make a 'wave moving path'. Just-in-
time calculation is out- sin takes too long.

But i bet in most cases this isn't the way it was done- instead,
some graph paper was taken, aome 'wave line' drawn on it (in math's
terms, this would be the graph of a sine function... but who cares?
We don't want to do math *ugh*, we want to do a cool demo.) and
taken a few values off it. Maybe 16 values per 'period' of the
wave...

Or, it was really done by 'trial and error', just fiddle about until
it looks right/ cool/ appropriate.

Another example: Remember Mandelbrot sets? Those 'apple men'? (i
think the 'appe man' has never made it into the english language-
but that thing really looks like an apple)

The formula behind it is just

A(n+1) = (A(n))² + c

where A(n+1) is the new A, A(n) the old one and C a constant; you
start with the actual 'coordinates' and look how the values A(n)
behave until, say, n=100. These are complex numbers (no, don't
ask...) and quite non-trivial maths. But the formula is really easy,
and the result looks pretty:

http://www.jjam.de/Java/Applets/Applets.html (sorry... site in
german; just klick 'Apfelmännchen' at the left)

So- yes, there is a lot of 'cheating' or simplifying especially in
demos. After all, that is what demo coding is all about (at least on
8-bit systems): squeeze something out of the hardware that couldn't
be done before. YOu *have* to cheat- or you loose ;-)

I ran across this Astrocade related project at AtariAge.com (this is a quote from the project's website):

"This is what I'm working on. It is a console that will replicate the classic consoles of the late 70's and early 80's [including the Astrocade]. At this time, I plan to release several different consoles, each with more advanced functionality."

Here's some more detailed information from the Retro-Console project website (http://www.retroconsole.com/):


A DESCRIPTION OF THE RETROCONSOLE PROJECT:

The RetroConsole is not yet available but it is currently in development. Actually it will be a set of products leading ultimately to a small, inexpensive console machine that plugs into a normal television and plays games from any of a number of 8-bit classic game consoles.

You will not be able to plug in cartridges or expansion items and it will probably not support all the different joysticks out there. Probably only one type, something popular like the psx gamepad, but an adapter to support classic joysticks is a possibility.

Instead, in order to play games, you will plug in a compact flash card (which can have up to a gigabyte of storage). First you will choose which system you want to simulate and then you will be able to choose which game you want to load. All roms you want to use will have to be transferred to a PC file and then loaded to the Compact Flash card. Legally, you only have the right to do this with any game you have actually purchased.

The system will be as simple as possible. There will be an fpga powerful enough to reimplement any of the 8-bit console systems and plenty of SRAM. The goal will be to reimplement the complete hardware for each console using VHDL. The systems will be implemented one at a time. The actual system and schematics if possible will be acquired. Then the system will be analyzed with logic analyzers. Technical documents and emulators such as MESS will be used to fill in details as necessary. But I will try to build each system as close to the genuine console as possible, reimplementing it chip by chip and swapping in the new implementation in a real console to make sure it works correctly.

There will be standard AV connectors and two standard joystick connectors. There will be standard ac and maybe battery support. And of course the compact flash interface. But other than that, there will not be other interfaces. It will be kept as simple and "plug and play" as possible. It is also possible that the system will be implemented in the form of a joystick as the TV GAMES (atari and midway) systems.

In order to allow different simulations to run, it will require programming the fpga with a cpu. I am considering if it will be possible to put in a microcontroller that will be able to program the fpga dynamically. This will add a great deal of complexity to the system. The microcontroller will have to access the compact flash, generate text for a ntsc output and program the fpga through JTAG. That will be a challenging side project so it is likely the first version of the Retro Console will have to be hooked to a PC in order to change console implementations.

HOW THIS IS DIFFERENT FROM EMULATION

Emulators use software to reproduce the functionality of hardware. There are timing issues and things that generally prevent emulators from being perfect. I have not seen the perfect emulator. If you find one, let me know. I was looking at Project64 the other day which is a terrific Nintendo64 emulator. I was amazed at how well it reproduced the N64 games. But I was playing Marty Party with my nephew when the emulator started to go haywire. There were weird graphic glitches and sometimes the camera would slow down to an absolute crawl. Most emulators have flaws such as this in places.

Still if you are not a classic gaming fanatic such as myself and just want to play a few casual games of your old system, I suggest you go over to http://www.mess.org and download the software. You run it right on your PC or even better you can build your own emulation-based "Retro Console" using one of these wonderful little mothers: http://www.mini-itx.com

What this project aims to do is reimplement the hardware of classic consoles using VHDL and FPGA technologies. For instance, the main processor of the Colecovision is a Zilog Z-80A running at a speed of 3.58 Mhz. The video display unit is a TMS9918A. These processors and other support chips will be reimplemented and consolidated into one FPGA. This is called creating a system on a chip and manufacturers do this all the time to reduce the manufacturing costs of electronic items. Though not exactly the same as the original console, VHDL will allow the new system to be an extremely close reproduction of the original because it will be built at the level of system gates.

This is already being done with great success by the way. There are projects out there that recreate a C64 on a chip, a VIC20, several 80's arcade games, a TRS-80, a Sinclair and an Atari 2600. I will add a links page to these projects shortly.

So to recap, creating a VHDL hardware representation of the console will be painstaking work, but the goal is to create perfect or near perfect reproductions that would make any discriminating classic gaming fan cheer.


Rather cool, don't you think?

You could as well have written

          JR   C, MINTO

Effectively, you have done MINTO+$-$ which happens to be the same as 
MONTO +($-$) which in turn is the same as MINTO+0 and, by definition 
of zero as the neutral element of addition (studied maths, you see!) 
MINTO+0 equals MINTO ;-)

OK, but why? What happens in this line?

JR is Z80's relative jump instruction and takes one byte as 
argument, called the displacement. The displacement is considered a 
signed integer (values above 127 are treated as negative numbers:255 
being -1, 254 being -2...) and -in case the jump is taken- added to 
the current program counter (which is represented in the assembler 
as the dollar sin). So, JR 0 gives no jump at all; JR 254 jumps back 
two bytes, just onto the 'JR' opcode- infinite loop ;-)

Obviously, if you give JR a label (which is almost always something 
bigger than 255) you get an error message, and if you don't you get 
the wrong binary output- you need to calculate the distance (the 
displacement byte) and use that as argument. This is what is done in 
your first example.

But ZMAC is one step intelligenter: If it sees a label, it does the 
calaculation autoMagically (Hey! Let the computer do the routine 
work!)- if you dig through assembler manuals, you will also come 
across conventions like

JR LABEL ; have the asembler calculate the displacement
JR +VALUE ; take VALUE as displacement byte- do not calculate on it!
JR -VALUE ; same for backwards jumps

Personally, i like the syntax 'jr abel' being converted 
automatically- saves lots of typing.
 
> It is the magic of lines like this that make the 
> code run from any memory location.

Not really... of course, if you can do without using absolute jumps 
(and calls!), you get a binary code snippet that will run 'as-is' 
from every location in memory (the term is 'relocatable')- but that 
is not true for the Bally 'integrated programs'.

The reason you can assemble them as cartridge files is just that a) 
they are designed to run in a ROM, and b) the assembler(!) keeps 
track of all the addresses. Just use a different ORG statement, and 
the code will be assembled to run at another memory location... in 
fact, that is (one of) the reasons why labels do exist: let the 
assembler program keep care of all your subroutine addresses.

(In case anyone should get the idea to rip the binary of one of the 
built-in programs, put it on a cartridge without any re-assembling, 
and claiming 'it runs! Without modification!'- yes, it will. But 
remember: The original is still in the console. As soon as 
the 'faked cartridge' gets to an absolute jump, or subroutine call, 
it will address it's built-in counterpart, not the cartridge 
space...)

Hope i have not taken off any of your admiration for the Bally 
programmers- they truly deserve it. But that the built-in programs 
will also run as cartridges if the source is compiled as such- that 
is not their fault (in fact, they'd have a hard time to prevent it i 
guess).

It's all a question of overall cost. If you do a board replacement

hundred-dollar price range (and if you are there already, you could 
as well save time and pre-invested money, and do it on the c-one 
reconfigurable computer)

Or, if you do plug-in replacements for Bally's custom chips, you'd 
have to a) find out what is actually needed (do all three burn out, 
or is it always the same single one?) and b) produce three mini-
boards, which maybe need each not only one FPGA, but also one ROM 
and some glue logic (remember- FPGA load their 'hardware behaviour' 
like a computer loads it's program into memory)

Another point to consider: low volume production is expensive! (in 
fact, the 300-boards first production run of the c-one had this 
reason. producing 200 Boards would have cost *more*, not only per-
board, but also total. Running smaller series will literally let the 
price explode- let alone finding a parts supplier that is willing to 
sell maybe 100 pieces of one part. A dozen is ok for hobbyists 
stores- but they might run out of stock on such numbers. And 
distributors won't sell you anything below several hundred- or only 
for insane prices.

Please don't get me wrong: I am not commercially involved into the c-
one project, nor do i want to discourage the Astrocade-FPGA-project.

Just keep the cost in mind, make sure someone has the necessary 
ammount of money to pre-finance the product (100 boards you say? can 
you drop below $100 apiece? Makes $10,000 investment without any 
profit!) and don't fall into creeping featuritis mode... it doesn't 
look too ood if you have to re-design everything just the moment you 
finally are ready-to-go because the main component has been 
discontinnued a week before. I'm following something like this on 
another project: lots of discussion of what to include and how to do

format for this stuff.  You could actually load this file in an XML
parser and, if configured correctly, type the information in there and
have it produce the file for you.  Anyway, I've typed up a few BASIC
programs, and I can't imagine that it's nearly as painful as using the
Bally keypad :-)

Not a problem, I can add a <DEC> tag that will allow you to do that.  It
may or may not be in the next version.  It depends on how burned out I
get fighting the checksum issue.  I'm adding 2 load formats and getting
the checksum to calculate correctly in 1 of them is giving me a
headache.  The reason that I have 2 formats is that Basic programs are
stored differently than data loads.  Sometimes the data loads are ML
programs and other times they are BASIC programs.  For instance,
Chicken's first load is a BASIC program that loads a ML program.
Haunted House, on the other hand, has a BASIC program that loads other
BASIC programs.  The first load uses interleaved bytes so that when the
BASIC program is loaded, the title screen loads simultaneously.  The
second load uses contiguous bytes that is purely the BASIC program.  The
load formats will handle all of these combinations gracefully.  I've
spent most of my day off battling some bugs in my code.  A couple of
BASIC decoding/encoding issues, more than my share of checksum issues.
But I'm getting closer.  There are certainly some things I'd like to
change about the file format too.  I don't think there is any reason to
have a HEADER and FOOTER tag, when I can just make them an attribute of
the LOAD tag.  We'll see where that ends up.  Anyway, I probably didn't

pieces, there's always hope. For the worst cases, i'd recommend 'ic

The AstroBASIC cart can be used to load data into various areas of memory if there's a RAM expansion available

Here's an explanation written by George Moses in 1982 in a letter to Richard Houser.  Remember, the Viper is a RAM expansion unit.  This is the complete letter:

    October 10, 1982

    Dick,

    Here are some cartridges on tape plus GraphixTablet in extended BASIC.
    To load cartridges use Astro BASIC and set your Viper Switches to "24-K" and non protected mode.  Load from tape with :INPUT %(24576) GO.  Wait for cursor (about 40 sec.).  Then throw the protect switch to the PROTECT mode and the range switch to "8-K."  RESET should bring up the menu.
    TO MAKE A COPY:
    Throw the range switch back to "24K" and use PRINT %(24576),4096 GO while recording.
    NOTE: You could also make a copy of your Viper Ext. BASIC this way at 2000 Baud.  Just load it with the Old Bally BASIC at 300 baud, swap cartridges, hit RESET, and follow the above directions!

    George

Some notes from Adam:

In the above letter:

1)  When using PRINT or INPUT, 24576 is $6000, which is where the Viper's RAM begins (I THINK that the Blue RAM starts at $5000).
2)  When using PRINT, 4096 is 4K, the size of whatever cart that was sent to Dick.

I GUESS if you used an input line like

:INPUT %(16384)

the program would be stored at the beginning of screen RAM.  If a machine language program wasn't going to use BASIC, and was small enough (and could be started automatically when loaded), then anywhere near the bottom of screen RAM could be used as storage as long as the program wasn't then overwritten with graphics.  That's a whole lot of Ifs...

You just need to dump your ROM to "tape" (but actually use the computer).  Once it's a WAV file, use Ballybin to clean it up.  At this point, Bob may be able to explain how to extract the 8K binary file.  If not, then don't worry.  Send the file to me, I'll send it to Mike White, he'll burn an 8K ROM.  He'll send the ROM to me and then I'll get it into the computer that way (yea, it's round-about, but it'll work).  Here's the command that you type into AstroBASIC to dump the BIOS to tape:

:PRINT %(0),%(4096)

It will take about 45 seconds, and then you're done.  Although it might LOOK like you only dumped 4K, you dumped all 8K, since BASIC works with words.

Anyway.  Now how do you tell which ROM you have?  Do you even have the 3164 ROM to help us out?  I've heard that version of the Bally Arcade has a red eject button.  Well, that may be a hint, but here's the real test.  This is an article that will help you figure-out what you've got.

From Arcadian, Vol. 5, No. 3, Pg. 49 (Jan. 14, 1983)

SNEAK UP AND BITE YA DEPARTMENT
-------------------------------
By Hoover Anderson Research and Design (H.A.R.D.)

By the time that volume 1, number 6 of ARCADIAN had hit the streets (May
1979) it was apparent that there were two configurations of on-board ROM.
Calls to some ROM subroutines worked on some machines but not on others.

H.A.R.D. has just spent an exasperating two months trying to produce game
tapes in 2000 baud Astrobasic that would load on the customer's machine.
The problem was that all PRINT statements in our programs were producing
characters that were offset by one letter AND one pixel on our customer's
machines: the string "ABC" would come out "BCD" and slightly off-center.

At first we thought it might be the tape quality. We spent a bundle having
custom cassettes loaded with high-quality Agfa PE-651 tape. No good... the
problem remained. We next suspected the recorder. Out went the trusty old
Panasonic Slimline to be replaced by a TRS-80 CCR-81 computer cassette
recorder. Still no dice... the characters remained jumbled on everyone
else's machine but our own. That was the worst part... we couldn't
duplicate the problem! Everything loaded worked perfectly in our own shop.
At the suggestion of one of our dealers , we even tried a new Astrobasic
cartridge. No deal... the problem would not go away. Finally, in
desperation, we bought another Arcade. Aha! We now had to Arcades sitting
side by side on the bench, and they couldn't talk to each other! There ARE
two different types of Arcades out there. The difference lies in the
on-board ROM, which is five bytes off-standard between the two. I have
christened these two machines "The 3159" and the "3164" based on the address
of the "GAME OVER" character string in each. A machine-language monitor
dump of the ROM was changed. Who knows why?... there was a bug fixed,
perhaps. Most of you have the 3159, but there are a number of you with the
3164 machines who are tearing your hear out or perhaps giving up in disgust
because you can't load anyone else's programs.

Here's a quick test. Type in the following on your Arcade:

CLEAR;
%(19904)=-43;%(19906)=12341;%(19908)=27651;%(19910)=3164;%(19912)=-13871;
CALL19904

If the words "GAME OVER" appear at the top of your screen, you've got the
3164 configuration and you are stuck. The newer 3159 configuration will
only print the word "OVER". If you change %(19910) to 3159, you will get
the entire "GAME OVER" on the 3159 machine.

END OF ARTICLE
